title: Voluntary jail healthcare accreditation improves care standards and reduces mortality without added capital or labor inputs
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 33357, randomized offer of healthcare accreditation across 46 U.S. jails
geography: United States; 46 midsized jails with average daily populations between 100 and 3,000

observations.period: Accreditation experiment; paper issued January 2025 and revised May 2026

denominator.unit: midsized U.S. jails randomized to immediate or delayed offer of National Commission on Correctional Health Care accreditation

quality_standard_compliance.unit: compliance with prespecified healthcare quality standards, especially training and patient care

twelve_month_mortality.unit: 12-month jail mortality; public abstract does not state the exact percentage estimate

capital_or_labor_inputs.unit: capital or labor inputs associated with the accreditation offer

operating_mechanisms.unit: reported mechanism evidence across staff, records, and medical audits

institutional_route.unit: standardized expertise and compliance assessment for publicly financed jail healthcare delivered by private contractors

observations.method: Randomized offer of NCCHC accreditation to 46 jails, comparing immediate versus delayed offer; compliance, organizational practice, mortality, staff, leadership, and medical-record measures were collected.
observations.uncertainty: The abstract reports improvements and mortality reduction but does not disclose every effect size, confidence interval, implementation cost, or long-run post-release outcome. The experiment identifies the offer pathway in selected midsized jails, not all correctional facilities or all forms of accreditation.
observations.subgroup: People detained in participating midsized jails, jail healthcare and custody staff, leadership, and contracted healthcare providers; people in custody rely on the institution for care and cannot freely switch providers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Accreditation may improve measured compliance without improving every unmeasured dimension of care; standards may redirect effort, impose administrative burden, or work differently where staffing, vendor, legal, or population conditions differ. A mortality effect does not establish post-release health, trust, or reduced detention exposure.

related_sources.claim: Official NBER DOI identifies the working paper.
NBER Reporter provides additional institutional and mechanism context for the accreditation experiment.

boundary: This record establishes an experimental institutional-practice-to-care-and-mortality route in selected U.S. jails. It does not establish post-release health, recidivism, household outcomes, trust, fairness of detention, contractor-wide performance, or general correctional-system effects.
